title: Where to Buy DHM: Online, In Stores, and What to Check First
excerpt: Where to buy DHM in the US: Amazon, iHerb, brand sites, and which stores (Walmart, CVS, Walgreens, GNC) sometimes stock it, plus how to check a label and compare prices.
metaDescription: Where to buy DHM: online vs. Walmart, CVS, Walgreens, and GNC, how to check stock near you, what to look for on the label, and how to compare prices.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the easiest and most reliable place to buy DHM in the US is online, mainly on Amazon, on large supplement sites like iHerb, or directly from the brand's own website. In physical stores, DHM is hit and miss. You may find a DHM-based hangover product at some Walmart, Target, CVS, Walgreens, GNC, Vitamin Shoppe, or Whole Foods locations, but stock varies a lot from store to store and many shelves don't carry it at all. If you need it tonight, check the store's app for in-store inventory before you drive over. If you can wait a day or two, buying online gets you far more choice and usually a lower price per dose.

**The quick rules:** Look for the amount of DHM (dihydromyricetin) per serving on the label, not just "Hovenia dulcis extract." Compare price per serving, not price per bottle. Buy from the brand's own store or the brand's official listing, not a random third-party seller. Be wary of any product that promises to "prevent" or "cure" hangovers. And if you take prescription medicine, ask your pharmacist before adding a new supplement.

> **This is not medical advice.** DHM is sold as a dietary supplement, which means the FDA does not review it for safety or effectiveness before it goes on sale. This guide covers where to buy it and how to judge a product, not whether it's right for you. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist first if** you take prescription medicine (especially sedatives, sleep aids, anti-anxiety drugs, or anything processed heavily by the liver), are pregnant or breastfeeding, have liver or kidney disease, or drink heavily most days. If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, such as confusion, vomiting they can't stop, slow or irregular breathing, a seizure, or they can't stay awake, call 911. No supplement helps with that.

## What You're Actually Shopping For

Before you go looking, it helps to know what DHM is, because products are labeled in a few different ways.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a flavonoid, a type of plant compound, found in the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*) and in some other plants, including a vine sometimes sold as "vine tea." Most DHM supplements are made from a concentrated extract that has been purified so that most of it is dihydromyricetin. You'll see it listed on labels in a few ways:

- **Dihydromyricetin** or **DHM**, with a dose in milligrams. This is the clearest labeling.
- **Hovenia dulcis extract** or **Japanese raisin tree extract**, sometimes with a percentage, like "standardized to 98% DHM." This is fine if the percentage is stated.
- **Hovenia dulcis fruit or seed extract** with no DHM percentage. This can be a much weaker product, because a plain plant extract may contain only a small amount of actual DHM.
- **Ampelopsin**, an older name for the same compound. Some labels use both.

Then there's the format. Some products are **pure DHM**, a single-ingredient capsule. Others are **hangover formulas** that combine DHM with other ingredients such as L-cysteine, milk thistle, prickly pear, B vitamins, and electrolytes. Neither type is automatically better. Single-ingredient products make it easy to know exactly what you're taking and tend to cost less per dose. Blends are convenient but harder to compare, and some include only a modest amount of DHM in a long list of ingredients. Our guide to [DHM product forms](/never-hungover/dhm-product-forms-absorption-comparison-2025) compares capsules, powders, and drinks in more detail.

A word on what DHM can and can't do, so you know what you're paying for: most of the research on DHM comes from animal and lab studies, which suggest it may affect how the body handles alcohol and how alcohol acts on the brain. Human evidence is limited and mixed. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers reliably in people, and it does not lower your blood alcohol level enough to make drinking safer or driving acceptable. Our [honest review of whether DHM works](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025) goes through what the studies actually found.

## Where to Buy DHM Online

Online is where you'll find the widest range of DHM products, and usually the best price per serving. Here are the main options and what to watch for with each.

### Amazon

Amazon carries nearly every major DHM brand, often with fast shipping. That makes it the most convenient choice for most people in the US. It also has the most noise. A search for "DHM" returns dozens of products, sponsored listings at the top, and a mix of established brands and unfamiliar names.

How to shop Amazon well:

- **Check who the seller is.** On the product page, look at "Ships from" and "Sold by." Ideally it's Amazon itself or the brand's own storefront. Third-party resellers can be fine, but they raise the chance of old stock, poor storage, or, rarely, counterfeit product.
- **Read the supplement facts panel in the images.** Don't rely on the title. Titles often say "1000mg" when that's the total of a blend, not the DHM.
- **Look at recent reviews, not just the star average.** A product can change its formula or manufacturer. Recent reviews that mention a different taste, smell, or capsule size can be a sign of that.
- **Be skeptical of review counts alone.** Review numbers tell you a product is popular, not that it works or is pure.

### iHerb and other large supplement retailers

iHerb, Vitacost, and similar online supplement stores carry a narrower selection of DHM than Amazon, but the products they stock usually come straight from the brand or a distributor. These sites can be a good option if you already shop there, and iHerb ships to many countries, which helps if you're outside the US.

### Direct from the brand

Many DHM brands sell on their own websites. Buying direct has a few advantages: you know the product came from the company, you can often find lot numbers or third-party test results posted on the site, and some brands offer subscriptions or bundle discounts. The downsides are that shipping can be slower or cost extra, and prices aren't always lower than on Amazon. If a brand posts a certificate of analysis (a lab report showing what's actually in a batch), that's a good sign.

### Specialty and smaller online shops

You'll also see DHM on smaller wellness sites, social media ads, and "hangover kit" subscription boxes. Some of these are legitimate. Others are drop-shipped products with vague labels and inflated prices. Apply the same tests as anywhere else: a clear DHM dose, a named manufacturer, a real return policy, and no miracle claims.

## Where to Buy DHM in Stores Near You

This is the part most people are actually searching for: can you walk into a store and buy DHM today? The honest answer is sometimes, and it depends heavily on where you live. Store selections change often, differ by location, and can differ between a chain's website and its physical shelves. The list below tells you where it's worth checking, not where you're guaranteed to find it.

### Pharmacies: CVS, Walgreens, Rite Aid

Big pharmacy chains stock lots of morning-after products: pain relievers, antacids, electrolyte drinks, and vitamin blends. Some locations also carry a branded hangover supplement, and a few of those contain DHM. Check the vitamin and supplement aisle and any seasonal "party" or "recovery" end cap. You're more likely to find these products in busy city or college-town stores than in small neighborhood ones. Our rundown of [hangover pills at CVS and Walgreens](/never-hungover/hangover-pills-at-cvs-walgreens) covers what's usually on those shelves and which products actually contain DHM.

If your store doesn't have a DHM product, the pharmacy aisle still has useful basics for the morning after, especially electrolyte drinks. Just don't pick up a "hangover" product without reading the ingredients. Many are a pain reliever plus caffeine, and some contain acetaminophen, which needs extra care after drinking.

### Big-box stores: Walmart and Target

Walmart and Target both sell supplements in stores and a much larger range online, including marketplace listings from outside sellers. Your best bet is to use the store app or website, search for "DHM" or "dihydromyricetin," and filter for in-store pickup at your location. That tells you quickly whether anything is actually on a nearby shelf. Keep in mind that items sold by third-party marketplace sellers on these sites usually ship from the seller and won't be in the store.

### Vitamin and supplement stores: GNC and The Vitamin Shoppe

Supplement chains are a reasonable place to look, because their staff and buyers follow supplement trends and they stock a broader range than pharmacies. Even so, DHM is a niche product, and many locations won't have it on the shelf. Both chains sell more online than in stores, and staff can sometimes order a product in for you. Call ahead rather than making a special trip.

### Natural grocers: Whole Foods, Sprouts, and independent health food stores

Natural and health food stores sometimes carry DHM or Hovenia dulcis products in their supplement section, particularly in larger cities. Independent health food stores are worth a phone call too. They often have more freedom to stock niche products, and some will special-order something if you ask.

### Liquor stores, gas stations, and convenience stores

You'll often see "hangover shots" and recovery drinks by the register at liquor stores, gas stations, and convenience stores. A few of them include DHM, often in small amounts alongside vitamins, electrolytes, and sugar. They're convenient but usually the most expensive way to get DHM per dose, and the labels are often vague about how much is actually in there. If you buy one, read the supplement facts panel and look for a stated DHM amount. See our roundup of [hangover shots](/never-hungover/best-hangover-shots) for how the common ones compare.

### Bars, festivals, and hotels

Some bars, festival vendors, and hotel shops sell single-serve hangover products at a steep markup. They're fine in a pinch. They're rarely good value.

### A simple plan if you need DHM today

1. Open the apps for the stores near you (Walmart, Target, CVS, Walgreens) and search "DHM" or "dihydromyricetin" with in-store pickup selected.
2. If nothing shows up, call your nearest GNC, Vitamin Shoppe, or independent health food store.
3. If that fails, order online with fast shipping, and plan ahead next time. DHM has a long shelf life when stored properly, so keeping a bottle at home saves the last-minute hunt.

## Buying Online vs. In a Store: Which Is Better?

For most people, online wins on choice and price, and in-store wins only on speed.

| Factor | Online (Amazon, iHerb, brand sites) | In-store (pharmacies, big-box, supplement shops) |
|---|---|---|
| Selection | Wide: pure DHM and many blends | Narrow, often one or two products or none |
| Price per serving | Usually lower, especially for larger bottles | Usually higher, especially single-serve items |
| Speed | Same day to a few days | Immediate, if it's in stock |
| Label checking | Must rely on product photos | Can read the bottle in person |
| Authenticity | Varies by seller; buy from the brand or official listing | Generally reliable from major chains |
| Returns | Depends on the seller | Usually easy at major chains |

If you plan to use DHM more than once in a while, buying a larger bottle online almost always works out cheaper than repeatedly buying single-serve products in stores.

## How to Tell if a DHM Product Is Worth Buying

Wherever you buy, the same handful of checks separate a reasonable product from a poor one. This matters more for supplements than for medicine, because supplements don't go through FDA approval before they're sold. The manufacturer is responsible for making sure the product is safe and labeled correctly, and quality varies.

### 1. A clear DHM dose per serving

The supplement facts panel should say how much dihydromyricetin (or a standardized extract with a stated percentage) is in each serving. Common doses on the market range from about 300 mg to 1,000 mg per serving. If the label only lists a "proprietary blend" with one total weight, you can't know how much DHM you're getting.

### 2. Purity or standardization

Many products state a purity, often 98%. That tells you the extract is mostly DHM rather than other parts of the plant. A product that says only "Hovenia dulcis extract" with no percentage may contain much less.

### 3. Third-party testing

Independent testing checks that what's on the label is in the bottle and that the product isn't contaminated with things like heavy metals or microbes. Some brands post certificates of analysis on their websites, and some products carry a seal from a testing program such as NSF or USP. Few DHM products have those seals, so a posted lab report from an independent lab is the more realistic thing to look for. Being made in a facility that follows Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) is a baseline, not a bonus.

### 4. A named company you can contact

A real brand lists a company name, an address, and a way to reach them. That matters if you have a reaction, a question about ingredients, or a problem with an order.

### 5. Honest marketing

Be cautious with products that promise to wipe out hangovers entirely or guarantee results every time, or that suggest you can drink as much as you like with no consequences. The research doesn't support those claims, and a company willing to make them may cut other corners too.

### 6. Fresh stock and an intact seal

Check the expiration date and make sure the safety seal is intact. Avoid bottles that have been sitting in a hot car or a sunny window display. Heat and moisture can degrade supplements over time.

## What DHM Costs, and How to Compare Prices

Prices change often, so think in terms of **price per serving** rather than the price on the sticker. A cheap bottle with few servings or a low dose can cost more per use than a bigger, pricier bottle.

To compare two products:

1. Divide the price by the number of servings to get price per serving.
2. Check how much DHM is in one serving.
3. If you want to compare strength too, divide price per serving by the DHM amount to get a rough cost per 100 mg or per 1,000 mg of DHM.

The pattern is clear: single-ingredient DHM in larger bottles tends to be the cheapest per dose, while multi-ingredient formulas and small packs cost more per use. That doesn't make blends a bad choice. You're paying for convenience and the other ingredients, which you may or may not want. ## Buying DHM Outside the US

DHM is sold in many countries, but the rules for supplements vary, and some countries regulate plant extracts and new food ingredients more strictly than the US does. A few general points:

- **Canada:** natural health products are regulated by Health Canada and need a product license, which shows up as an eight-digit Natural Product Number (NPN) on the label. A product without one may not be authorized for sale there.
- **UK and Europe:** rules for food supplements and new ingredients are stricter than in the US, and availability on store shelves is limited. Many people order from online retailers that ship internationally.
- **Australia:** the Therapeutic Goods Administration regulates many supplements, and products sold locally may be listed with them. Personal imports from overseas are subject to their own rules.
- **Asia:** Hovenia dulcis has a long history of traditional use in parts of East Asia, and related products are more common in stores there, but labeling and dose information vary.

If you're ordering from abroad, check your country's customs and import rules for supplements, expect longer shipping times, and factor in import duties. Our [worldwide DHM availability guide](/never-hungover/dhm-availability-worldwide-guide-2025) has more country-by-country detail.

## Red Flags to Avoid When Buying DHM

Most DHM products on the market are ordinary supplements from ordinary companies. But a few warning signs are worth knowing:

- **No DHM amount on the label**, or only a vague "proprietary blend."
- **Prices far below everyone else's** for the same product, especially from an unfamiliar seller. That can mean old stock, a counterfeit, or a product that doesn't contain what it says.
- **Missing or tampered safety seals.**
- **Unclear company information**, no address, or no way to contact a real person.
- **Big medical claims**, such as protecting your liver from any amount of drinking, curing hangovers, or replacing medical treatment.
- **Pressure tactics**: countdown timers, "only 3 left" banners that never change, or auto-renewing subscriptions that are hard to cancel.
- **Undisclosed stimulants or drugs.** Some "hangover" products include caffeine or over-the-counter pain relievers. That's not necessarily bad, but you need to know so you don't double up with something else you're taking.

## Before You Buy: Is DHM Right for You?

Buying DHM is easy. Deciding whether to take it deserves a minute of thought.

DHM is generally well tolerated in the small amount of human research available, and side effects reported are usually mild. But long-term safety data in people is limited, and there's very little research on how it interacts with medicines. Animal research suggests DHM acts on GABA receptors, the same brain system targeted by alcohol, benzodiazepines, and some sleep aids, so caution with sedating medications makes sense. It may also affect how the liver processes some drugs. That's why the advice to check with a pharmacist if you take prescription medicine matters. Our [DHM safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-safety-complete-guide-2025) and [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) cover this in more detail.

A few practical points:

- **DHM is not a license to drink more.** It does not make drunk driving safe, and it won't protect you from alcohol poisoning.
- **Hydration, food, sleep, and pacing still matter most.** No supplement replaces drinking less, slowing down, eating beforehand, and having water between drinks.
- **Timing and dose:** most people who use DHM take it while drinking or before bed. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) walks through common approaches.

## Our Picks if You're Buying DHM Online

If you've decided to try DHM and want a straightforward place to start, here are two products from our reviews that are easy to find on Amazon. We earn a small commission if you buy through these links, at no extra cost to you, and our rankings are based on label quality, dose, and price per serving.

- **For value and a simple, single-ingredient formula:** [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) lists 1,000 mg of DHM per serving and is one of the lowest-cost options per dose among the products we track. The trade-off is that it's DHM only, with no extra ingredients, which is a plus or a minus depending on what you want.
- **For an all-in-one formula:** [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) combines DHM with L-cysteine, milk thistle, and other ingredients. It costs noticeably more per serving and comes in a smaller pack, so it suits occasional use more than frequent use.
- **For a lower dose to start with:** [DHM Depot](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0767N448Q?tag=dhmguide-20) lists 300 mg per capsule, which makes it easy to adjust how much you take.

For side-by-side scores on more brands, see our [DHM supplement reviews](/reviews). Whichever you choose, check the seller, read the label, and keep realistic expectations. DHM is a promising compound with limited human evidence, not a hangover cure.

## The Bottom Line

- The most reliable place to buy DHM in the US is online: Amazon, large supplement retailers like iHerb, or the brand's own website.
- In stores, DHM is possible but unpredictable. Check pharmacy, big-box, supplement-store, and natural-grocer apps for in-store stock before you go.
- Compare price per serving and DHM per serving, not bottle price.
- Choose products with a clear DHM dose, a stated purity, a named company, and ideally independent lab testing.
- Avoid products with vague labels, miracle claims, or suspiciously low prices from unknown sellers.
- If you take prescription medicine, are pregnant, or have liver or kidney disease, talk to your pharmacist or doctor before you start.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Where can I buy DHM?**

In the US, the easiest places are online: Amazon, large supplement retailers like iHerb, and brand websites. Some Walmart, Target, CVS, Walgreens, GNC, Vitamin Shoppe, and natural grocery stores carry DHM-based products, but availability varies a lot by location. Check each store's app for in-store stock before you go.

**Can you buy DHM at Walmart, CVS, or Walgreens?**

Sometimes. These chains occasionally stock a hangover supplement that contains DHM, and their websites list more products than their shelves do. Search "DHM" or "dihydromyricetin" in the store app with in-store pickup selected for your location. If nothing shows up, ordering online is usually faster than driving between stores.

**Does GNC or The Vitamin Shoppe sell DHM?**

Supplement chains are a reasonable place to look, but DHM is a niche product and many locations won't have it on the shelf. Both chains sell more online than in stores. Call your local store first, and ask whether they can order it in if they don't stock it.

**Is it safe to buy DHM on Amazon?**

Generally yes, if you buy from the brand's own storefront or from listings shipped and sold by Amazon. Check the seller information on the product page, read the supplement facts panel in the photos rather than trusting the title, and be wary of prices far below other sellers. Look for a clear DHM dose and, ideally, a brand that posts independent lab test results.

**How much does DHM cost?**

Prices vary widely. Single-ingredient DHM in larger bottles tends to cost the least per serving, often well under a dollar or two per dose, while blends and single-serve shots cost more. Compare price per serving and the amount of DHM per serving rather than the price of the bottle.

**What should I look for on a DHM label?**

Look for the amount of dihydromyricetin per serving in milligrams, or a Hovenia dulcis extract with a stated DHM percentage. A purity figure, a named manufacturer with contact details, GMP manufacturing, and an independent lab report are all good signs. Avoid labels that hide the DHM amount in a proprietary blend.

**Is DHM the same as Hovenia dulcis or Japanese raisin tree extract?**

Not exactly. DHM is a compound found in the Japanese raisin tree (Hovenia dulcis) and some other plants. An extract labeled "standardized to 98% DHM" is mostly DHM, but a plain Hovenia dulcis extract with no percentage may contain much less. Check the label for the actual DHM amount.

**Do I need a prescription to buy DHM?**

No. In the US, DHM is sold as an over-the-counter dietary supplement. That also means it isn't reviewed by the FDA for safety or effectiveness before sale, so it's worth talking to a pharmacist or doctor first if you take prescription medicine, are pregnant, or have liver or kidney disease.
